https://www.dw.com/en/russia-why-is-the-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IiKB Yabloko Party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov attending a hearing at the Russian Supreme Court to disqualify Yabloko from the 2026 State Duma election Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement On Monday Russia's supreme court upheld a lawsuit against the anti-war opposition party Yabloko. Its candidates will now be barred from taking part in the parliamentary elections on September 18 to 20. The case against Yabloko was brought by the pro-Kremlin party Rodina, which accused it of infringing copyright with its election campaign materials. Rodina also made the claim that Yabloko had engaged in extremist activities and had received illegal financing from abroad. The verdict was pronounced by presiding judge Vyacheslav Kirillov. This was the same judge who, in April, banned the Russian human rights organization Memorial and designated it an extremist organization. Kirillov also previously dismissed legal complaints against the Russian prison service filed by the prominent opposition politician Alexei Navalny . Navalny spent many years in Russian prisons prior to his death in jail in 2024. At least 500 people gathered in front of the Supreme Court to show their support for Yabloko. They distributed apples and sang songs. The name Yabloko – "apple" in English – derives from the initials of the party's three founders, Grigory Yavlinsky, Yury Boldyrev and Vladimir Lukin (YaBL). The apple is now well-known as a symbol of the party. At the end of the nine-hour court session, security services threatened the people gathered outside the courthouse with arrest, also warning young men that they could be taken to an army enlistment office. Several hundred people, most of them young, gathered outside the Supreme Court to await the outcome of the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance "You are mistaken if you believe that, with a stroke of a pen, you can write off millions of people who want peace, freedom and a normal future for their country," Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Yabloko, wrote on Telegram that evening. He insisted that the party had not broken any Russian laws, and announced that he would appeal the judgement. The Kremlin 'got scared' Grigory Yavlinsky, one of the founders of Yabloko, said those in power were afraid of Yabloko's program, which calls for an election "for peace, freedom and a life without fear" – because, he said, "removing a party with a platform like this from the election, without any real grounds, is the political system exposing itself." The lawsuit came at the same time as an appeal by Russian opposition and cultural leaders living abroad for people to support Yabloko. They include the politician Yulia Navalnaya , Alexei Navalny's widow, as well as Lyubov Sobol, Ilya Yashin and Andrei Pivovarov. The writer Dmitry Bykov, human rights activist Oleg Orlov and other prominent people also voiced their support for Yabloko. Navalnaya, who now leads the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) her husband set up in 2011, responded to the verdict. The Kremlin was originally going to let Yabloko stand in the elections, she said, but those in power "got scared" and had the party blocked. Navalnaya wrote on Telegram that the powers-that-be had observed a development they wanted to stop at any cost: People were starting to join forces. This, she wrote, was less about support for Yabloko than the possibility for millions of Russians to express how they really felt about Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine. Andrei Pivovarov, a political activist who lives in exile in Germany and is a coordinator of the Russian Antiwar Committee , explained to DW that the opposition had not believed supporting Yabloko would bring about swift political change or an end to the war. The aim, he said, had been to make visible the extent of anti-war sentiment in Russia. "There would have been a dozen parties on the ballot who are pro-war, and one that is pro-peace. The war wouldn't end even if Yabloko were to get representatives into the State Duma. But we would have seen that a lot of Russians oppose the war," said Pivovarov. This view, he added, would not simply disappear now Yabloko has been barred from standing. What were the Kremlin's plans for Yabloko? The political scientist Ivan Preobrazhensky speculated in an interview with DW that the banning of Yabloko could be a consequence of a power struggle between different interest groups in the Kremlin. He suggested that the security bloc allied with the federal security service, the FSB, may have wanted Yabloko to act as a counterweight to the New People party. This is regarded as a project of Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of the presidential administration. Another version of events is that Kiriyenko himself may have tried to create the impression of political rivalry, and underestimated the potential of anti-war feeling in the country. Yabloko party chairman Rybakov (right) with his lawyer, during the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance Preobazhensky says the government underestimated the number of people in Russia who oppose the war and are ready to support a political force campaigning for an end to the war in Ukraine . Surveys, he says, indicate that there is substantial demand for such a political alternative. He also believes that the Kremlin initially intended to let Yabloko run in the election but changed its mind when it saw how much support the party was getting. Another political scientist, Mikhail Vinogradov, thinks there was a different calculation behind the move. If Yabloko had scored very few votes in the election, the Kremlin could have painted a picture of a population solidly behind the war. A poor result would also have served to disillusion those who oppose it. Barring Yabloko makes independent election monitoring more difficult. The party is now no longer allowed to send representatives to monitor polling stations. Roman Udot, a Russian specialist in electoral observation, explains that Yabloko has also enabled access for independent observers in the past. Does the Kremlin have the situation under control? The State Duma elections are taking place at a time of growing uncertainty in Russian society, says Margarita Zavadskaya from the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. She points to data from the Russian Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), which regularly records the population's prevailing view of the situation in the country: optimism or alarm? At the end of July, 57% of those surveyed said that they were worried. This is the highest level since mobilization in the autumn of 2022. FOM surveys should be taken with a grain of salt, but Zavadskaya says an increase like this in high summer indicates that "something is not going according to plan." She gives the increase in drone attacks, deaths, fires in warehouses and rumors of a fresh mobilization as the reasons, and comments that the summer of 2026 has been the most unsettling for the people in Russia since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. She also believes the number of people who support the war is going down rather than up. The Russian leadership therefore has good reason to be nervous. "For the Kremlin, the ideal scenario would be a boring election with low turnout and no noteworthy events," says Zavadskaya. "Right now, though, this seems unlikely, as the situation in the run-up to the election does not appear normal, nor does it give the impression that the government has the situation under control." https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: ABU DHABI — After a nine-month break, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met to restart face-to-face talks on how to end the four-and-a-half-year war, with tentative signs of early progress. The two sides discussed an exchange of prisoners, but contrary to some reports, it has not yet been finalized, according to one official familiar with the matter, who was granted anonymity because the meeting was confidential. The talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday focused on what security guarantees Ukraine — and Russia — want to see after the war ends. On the second and final day of the meeting on Wednesday, negotiators are due to turn to the highly sensitive question of territory. Privately, U.S. officials who convened the meeting say both Russia and Ukraine have shown at least some readiness to be flexible on the issue of land. Advertisement Advertisement The meeting with Russia and the U.S. was “constructive and quite substantive,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy posted on X after receiving a report from his negotiating team. “They had time to discuss the need and possible parameters for humanitarian steps. The release of prisoners is a priority.” Zelenskyy said the negotiating teams spoke “in detail” about what security guarantees would be required to stop Russia from attacking Ukraine again in the future. In a significant move toward easing Ukraine’s fears, the U.S. is asking the Russian side if they would consent to America providing Ukraine with NATO-like commitments to collective defense, or even for NATO to sign such an agreement itself. “Real tools are needed to block any recurrence of the war,” Zelenskyy said. According to Russian state media, the talks ended after 4.5 hours and were conducted in Russian. Alongside the Ukrainian and Russian negotiators, the United Arab Emirates foreign minister and NATO’s top commander in Europe were also at the table. Earlier in the day, European representatives held talks with the American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, who convened the negotiations. The European side agreed with the Americans to review Europe's wider security architecture as part of the peace process for Ukraine — a step toward meeting one of Russia's central demands. “It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the G-7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard. It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dekoder.org/de/gnose/indepen.text: Gnose (Was ist das?) Independence a la Ukraine National flag and Independence Monument (since 2001) featuring Berehynya and a kalyna branch on Maidan Nesaleshnosti in Kyiv / © Peggy Lohse/dekoder Ukrainians have fought and died for their country’s independence. They are doing so today, on the front lines or under Russian airstrikes behind them. For over a decade, they have been doing so in the underground resistance in annexed or occupied territories and in battles with Russian-supported separatists. In earlier eras, they died in famines exacerbated by Moscow, from KGB bullets and in Soviet labour camps. In the 20th century, Ukrainian nationalists fought against Russia but also – sometimes alongside German National Socialists – against Jewish and Polish communities in their own country. Before that, though, there were also those who envisioned a Soviet Ukraine that was independent – whether in a civic-nation model or a federal model. This pursuit of state sovereignty at all costs: where does it come from? How has the Ukrainian concept of statehood changed over time? Ukrainian historian Andrii Portnov outlines the historical development of ideas and practices of an independent Ukraine over the past two centuries up to the present day. The first piece of our new dossier in English: Ukraine Basics . Original 22. Mai 2025 von Andrii Portnov Übersetzung von Alison Borrowman Chapters There was no country by the name of Ukraine to be found on the political map of Europe at the start of the 19th century. The Russian Empire had destroyed the last elements of the Cossack Hetmanate in the late 18th century. However, the absence of a state structure should not be equated with the absence of a nationalist movement. Inspired by the ideas of Herder and other Romantic philosophers, the Ukrainian intelligentsia proposed a project aimed at the cultural and political emancipation of the Ukrainian-speaking rural population of both existing empires, tsarist Russia and the Austro-Hungarian empire. Drahomanov: Stateless Ukraine predestined for “ideal federalism” One of the key figures of Ukrainian political thought in the 19th century was Mykhailo Drahomanov , an ancient historian who was forced to emigrate from the Russian Empire in 1876 due to his political beliefs. In exile, Drahomanov published the journal Hromada (Eng: Community) in Geneva and, in 1889, became the head of the world history programme at the University of Sofia. In Drahomanov’s view, Ukraine, having, for historical reasons, neither an upper class nor its own state, was ideally suited for the socialist “practices of the stateless order”. And Ukrainians, he felt – “the most numerous of the peasant nationalities of Eastern Europe” – should play a key role in making an ideal federalism a reality. The “ideal”, here, consisted in the enjoyment of equal rights by all nationalities. Drahomanov called on both the Polish and the Russian socialist movements to recognise the ethnocultural independence of Ukrainians and renounce any imperialist ambitions. For Drahomanov, Ukrainian statehood was not the paramount aim. On the contrary, he argued that national unity within one state did not necessarily lead to greater freedom, using Germany as his example. He also called on both the Polish and the Russian socialist movements to recognise the ethnocultural independence of Ukrainians and renounce any imperialist ambitions. Baсhynsky: The nation-state as necessary stage in the socialist revolution The first theoretical justification for the political independence of Ukraine appeared in 1895, from the pen of the Lviv-based Marxist Yulian Bachynsky . In his essay Ukraina Irredenta , Baсhynsky attempted to apply Friedrich Engel’s analysis of the class character of the state to the Ukrainian context. Baсhynsky compared the Ukrainian question to the Irish question, concluding that “Ukraine’s political independence is a sine qua non for its economic and cultural development, a condition for the very possibility of its existence.” 1 This political independence would apply to “everyone who lives in Ukraine”, regardless of ethnicity or religion. According to Bachynsky political independence would apply to “everyone who lives in Ukraine”, regardless of ethnicity or religion. Taking a cue from Engels, Bachynsky pointed out that the nation-state was a necessary stage of societal development and an inevitable product of capitalist conditions. Accordingly, he considered Ukrainian political independence to be a necessary precondition for the formation of a Ukrainian bourgeoisie and hence for the accelerated creation of conditions intensifying the class struggle and the socialist revolution. Lypynsky: A nation of citizens The overthrow of the monarchy and the democratic February Revolution in 1917 in Russia created an opportunity for the Ukrainian intelligentsia to implement the ideals of socialism, federation and the right to national self-determination. The Ukrainian People’s Republic, proclaimed in Kyiv, had not yet survived for a year when it fell to the military aggression of the Russian Bolsheviks. Starting in 1918, Ukraine experienced a kaleidoscope of regime changes, foreign (German, Polish, French) intervention, peasant uprisings, and anti-Jewish pogroms. With the signing of the Treaty of Riga in March 1921, a new Polish–Soviet border was established: the Ukrainian provinces of the former Russian Empire (with the exception of Volhynia ) were recognised as part of Soviet Ukraine under Bolshevik rule, while the western Ukrainian territories that had previously belonged to the Austrian Empire were ceded to the Polish Republic, which had been reestablished in 1918. For Lypynsky, “all inhabitants of this country and all citizens of this state” were members of the Ukrainian nation. The defeat of the Ukrainian Revolution, in which socialist and federalist rhetoric had played a prominent role, led to a painful reassessment of the tasks and methods of the Ukrainian movement. Viacheslav Lypynksy , a Christian-conservative thinker, proposed some original approaches in this context. Lypynsky, who had been shocked by the experiences in the revolutionary years 1917-1921, categorically rejected both democracy and socialism. But national exceptionalism and chauvinism had no place in his vision for the future of Ukraine either: for Lypynsky, “all inhabitants of this country and all citizens of this state” were members of the Ukrainian nation. Lypynsky, himself born into a Polish noble family, emphasized that “anyone who wants the Ukraine to no longer be a colony is a Ukrainian” – i.e. anyone who advocated the establishment of a Ukrainian state. Lypynsky’s fundamentally integrative approach strongly influenced the further development of Ukrainian political thought. The Crimean Archipelago A Multimedia Dossier read here Dontsov, Bandera & the Second World War: Radicalisation in the struggle for Ukrainian statehood However, Lypynsky’s influence proved unable to match that of another political theorist in the interwar years of the 1920s and 1930s: Dmytro Dontsov , a zealous advocate of national exclusivity and the ruthless struggle for independent statehood in his book Nationalism 2 , which was published in Lviv in 1926. The constant in Dontsov’s work is a radical anti-Russian attitude. His writings are rife with militant antisemitism and racism, and the influence of German National Socialism is palpable. Dontsov’s central theses match the rhetoric of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists , which was established in1929 with the declared aim of fighting for Ukrainian sovereignty. Rejecting the methods of legal democratic politics on principle, the OUN operated in the underground, concentrating on young people. The young nationalists saw inter-ethnic relations as a destructive struggle for existence in the social Darwinist sense. Rejecting any notion of the rule of law, the OUN wanted the borders established after the First World War to be redrawn and hence sought contact with Germany, which also had a direct interest in shifting state boundaries. With an eye to Mussolini’s Italy and Hitler Germany, the OUN advocated a single party dictatorship and the Führerprinzip (“leader principle”). In 1940, the organisation split into two fractions, each taking its name from its leader: the Banderivtsi (OUN-B, for Stepan Bandera ) and the Melnykivtsi (OUN-M, for Andrii Melnyk ). The constant in Dontsov’s work is a radical anti-Russian attitude. The German invasion of the Soviet Union began on 22 June 1941, and the Wehrmacht marched into Lviv on 30 June. The same day, the OUN-B declared the “restoration of the Ukrainian state” in that city. As this was done without the permission of the German authorities, Bandera (in Kraków at the time) and Yaroslav Stetsko , his second-in-command, were arrested and interned in a special barrack in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp (where they continued to be held until September 1944). The complicity of some Ukrainian nationalists in the Nazi holocaust and the ethnic cleansing of the Polish population in Volhynia that the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) initiated are the darkest pages in the history of the Ukrainian underground. The OUN’s authoritarian methods drew criticism from Ukrainian émigré thinkers early in post-war years. In particular, the philosopher Vasyl Rudko described the casual sacrifice of human lives for the sake of the abstract slogan of a people’s revolution as being characteristic of the OUN and argued that Dontsov’s ideology had paved the way for totalitarianism and a cult of violence. The historian Borys Krupnytsky also wrote of the dangers of modern national socialism in the late 1940s. Khvylovy: “Independent republican organism as part of the Soviet Union”? The Second World War led to the transfer of the western Ukrainian territories that had belonged to Poland until 1939 to Soviet Ukraine. In other words, it was Stalin – the politician responsible for the Holodomor of 1932–33 and mass repression – who realised the age-old aim of the Ukrainian movement: the unification of all Ukrainian territories within a single state. The state in question – the Soviet Union – had been established in 1922, with Soviet Ukraine as one of its founding republics. Although they had installed Soviet rule in Ukraine through force of arms, the Bolsheviks recognised the mobilisation potential inherent in the Ukrainian national movement, the Ukrainian language and Ukrainian nationality. In the 1920s, Soviet Ukraine appeared to be the desirable form of Ukrainian statehood in the eyes of many people. “Ukraine is independent not because we Communists desire it to be, but because the iron and irresistible will of the laws of history demands it …” Mykola Khvylovy The writer Mykola Khvylovy , for instance, wrote the following in his 1926 pamphlet Ukraine or Malorossia? ( Malorossia or Little Russia was a pejorative name used by Great Russia (Russia itself) to define the territory of Ukraine as smaller and less powerful – dekoder): “We are indeed an independent state, one whose republican organism is part of the Soviet Union. And Ukraine is independent not because we Communists desire it to be, but because the iron and irresistible will of the laws of history demands it, because only in this way can we hasten class differentiation in Ukraine.” By the end of the decade though, the Soviet government had already prohibited the expression of such views, most of Ukraine’s cultural elites had become the targets of repression and a programme of Russification was implemented in the education system, including measures aimed at bringing the Ukrainian language closer to Russian. Although these trends intensified over time, the Soviet Union never abolished Ukraine’s status as a republic, nor did it eradicate the independence of the Ukrainian language and nationality. Presidential elections in Ukraine, 2019 rounds, regions, results read here Since 1991: Democratic independence and the Soviet legacy In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed along the borders of 15 Soviet republics. In Ukraine’s case, the deliberate decision of the local elites of the Communist Party of Ukraine (CPU) to separate from Moscow and seek an independent existence played a key role in this. In 1992, Deutsche Bank published a report 3 assessing Ukraine as one of the former Soviet republics with the best conditions for economic growth and political and social development, due to its industrialisation, the high level of education of its population and its natural resources. The high economic expectations combined with the deep disappointment in the planned economy in the late Soviet period as well as the noticeable shortages of many goods go a long way towards explaining the striking results of the referendum on Ukrainian independence that was held on 1 December 1991: 92.3 of voters cast their ballots in favour of independence, with a voter turnout of 84.2 percent. The new state granted citizenship automatically to every person residing in its territory, irrespective of ethnicity or language skills. That same day, Leonid Kravchuk , the former secretary of the CPU, was elected to serve as the newly independent Ukraine’s first president. The identity of the first person to fill this office was important: it signified that the new state was the outcome not of a revolution but of a democratic process that played out on the foundations of the old Soviet institutions. Independent Ukraine inherited borders defined by the Soviet expansionist policy, Soviet Ukraine’s industrial and transport infrastructure and a host of social, economic and cultural problems created by Soviet policies. The new state granted citizenship automatically to every person residing in its territory, irrespective of ethnicity or language skills. Moreover, Ukraine gave up the Soviet nuclear weapons that were stationed on its territory in 1994. At the time, this seemed to be the only appropriate response to the painful experience of the 1986 Chernobyl accident and the general agreement on the necessity of further nuclear disarmament. It is worth mentioning that despite all its economic and other problems, independent Ukraine did, unlike Russia and Belarus, succeed in establishing a political system featuring regular changes of government and competitive elections. Ukraine has held seven presidential elections since December 1991, and six different people have taken up the office in that period. By way of comparison: in Belarus, the office of president was held by one person in the 1994–2024 period and three people served as president over that period in Russia. Despite its economic and other problems, independent Ukraine did, unlike Russia and Belarus, succeed in establishing a political system featuring regular changes of government and competitive elections. No blood was spilled in connection with Ukraine’s separation from the USSR in December 1991. Nor was physical violence a significant factor in the subsequent political development of independent Ukraine. This changed 2014, first with the Euromaidan in January and then with Russia’s annexation of Crimea in March and the outbreak of the war in the Donbas in April. Russia’s full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022 and the ability of Ukrainian society to defend itself against it have led many observers to describe the current Russia-Ukraine war as a war over the political and cultural independence of Ukraine.
